articleTitle: A methodology for strategic plan modelling
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: This paper describes a methodology aimed at the resolution of the large-scale project planning problem. The methodology concentrates on the system identification problem. This is viewed as a means of portraying the large-scale project as a human activity system. With this type of system the essential features which need to be modelled are those of mission statement and infrastructure. Recognising that the means by which successful large-scale project management is carried out are negotiation and collaboration, and that these require a different modelling paradigm to that used for thermodynamic systems, the methodology embodies a semantic approach, somewhat akin to that found in artificial intelligence. Using a type of conceptual graph to characterise the components of large-scale project design such as mission statement, management structure support, partner involvement, and project work-package structure, the paper outlines a methodology for the interpretation of these graphs. The planning problem is defined as the determination (dynamically) of that mission statement and supporting infrastructure which best serves partners' interests in order to achieve those (high level) deliverables for which the project was originally conceived. A description of the application of this methodology to a real large-scale project is included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: The current generation of planning systems cannot cope with problems containing extensive disjunction. This paper describes an approach in which multiple alternatives can be handled efficiently by using techniques which identify and eliminate nonviable routes between the start point and the goal. The method relies on a set of supplementary data structures linked to route-defining branch labels, and exploits the concept of selection utility in the process of choosing desirable plans from among allowable alternatives.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: Concerns the preparation by Rediffusion of a bid for a contract to build a flight simulator for pilot training. The explicit inclusion of a component or components may lead to implicit requirements too, and unless there is a detailed accounting system then errors will occur. Much depends on the experience and skill of the sales engineer or project manager involved. The goal of the research programme was to engineer an expert system environment to provide a means of representing and reasoning about the structure and interrelation of component parts and their integration. The knowledge for the system has been extracted from experienced project managers, product engineers and sales engineers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Corporate and information systems planning-the missing links
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: A common set of questions expressed in business terms can provide a single driving force to which all activities to implement a company's IT vision and to integrate business and IT functions can be linked. The questions derive from the interests and concerns of the most senior management. The outcome is a shared IT vision and a common planning and management framework which complements organisation structure and culture and is closely integrated with the way in which other functions of the business are planned and managed. Additionally, matters of policy, e.g. investment authorisation procedures, rules for charging for IS/IT services and adoption of national or industry standards are clarified. Addressing these issues at an early stage greatly simplifies the derivation of IS and IT strategies and greatly improves the probability of successful implementation and business satisfaction in IT investment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: Summary form only given. A general description of planning is followed by a discussion of principles of computer-assisted planning. The importance of quality assurance is considered. A concept of neatness of results is examined. Methods of plan building are considered. The procedure is to predict, to manage and to monitor. Problems in using intelligent tools are outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: The space industry is oriented towards the achievement of specific goals. It stands on its record of achievement, both in the sense of facing its own future and with regard to its need for methodologies. The author reviews the importance of goal selection and maintenance. Examples are used to illustrate how space systems projects are run. Current trends that may give rise to changes of approach are highlighted, and areas where change might be appropriate are categorised.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Executive decision support systems, business goal seeking
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Goal-Driven Planning in Complex Environments
abstract: Group business and business unit managements face the complex task of linking the needs of and performance targets for shareholders to the business operating and reporting systems and the related management decision processes. To develop an expert system to help with a decision support process means focusing on the decisions involved. It is possible to develop an expert system to support the decision processes by studying the decision process and the goals which a business is normally expected to achieve. It is then possible to arrange data and other information needed in relation to the decision-taking process. The article describes how this may be done, and discusses applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
